summary: Specifies a stateless way for providers to deploy IPv6-only network domains while still offering IPv4 service. IPv4 TCP and UDP packets also work as valid IPv6 packets while crossing the domain. It is experimental.

subtitle: Tunnel IPv4 packets through IPv6-only networks while preserving transparency.

tldr.problem: As networks transition to IPv6-only, service providers need a way to keep offering IPv4 service to customers without maintaining state in gateway nodes.
tldr.mechanism: 4rd reversibly translates IPv4 packet headers into valid IPv6 headers so TCP and UDP packets traverse IPv6 networks unchanged, then translates back at the exit.
tldr.outcome: IPv6-only domains can support both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic without additional gateways, and customers can share public IPv4 addresses using restricted port sets.

facts.value: Translates IPv4 packets to IPv6 format

today: RFC 7600 is an experimental RFC and has not been adopted as a standard. It represents a possible approach to stateless IPv4-over-IPv6 tunneling but remains a research proposal for the networking community.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem
sections.content:
Service providers face a challenge: they want to deploy IPv6-only networks to simplify infrastructure and reduce costs, but they must continue to support IPv4 service to customers because IPv4 is still widely used on the Internet. Previous solutions like RFC 5969 (6rd) tunneled IPv6 packets through IPv4 networks, but the reverse is harder because IPv6 headers are much larger than IPv4 headers.

4rd solves this with a stateless approach: the provider does not need to keep per-customer records in gateway nodes. Instead, the protocol uses reversible packet translation—each IPv4 packet is translated into an IPv6 packet in a way that can be precisely reversed, preserving the original IPv4 data. During the journey across the IPv6 network, the packet looks like a normal IPv6 packet to all the routing and inspection machinery.
sections.plainLanguage: Service providers want to use only IPv6 networks but still support customers using IPv4. 4rd translates IPv4 packets into IPv6 format for the journey, then back to IPv4, without needing the network to remember anything about each customer.

sections.title: How 4rd Works
sections.content:
A 4rd domain is an IPv6 network with one or more Border Relays (BRs) that connect to the public IPv4 Internet, and Customer Edge (CE) routers at customer sites. Each CE is assigned an IPv6 prefix. Using mapping rules (which can be announced via stateless DHCPv6), the CE derives a 4rd IPv4 prefix from that IPv6 prefix.

When a CE sends an IPv4 packet destined for another IPv4 address, it translates the packet headers reversibly into IPv6 format and routes it toward the IPv6 network. Other CEs can reach each other directly (mesh topology) or via the BRs (hub-and-spoke). A BR translates packets back to IPv4 when they exit the domain.

The key property is that during the IPv6 journey, the packet remains valid for IPv6 tools like firewalls and packet inspectors. The checksum of TCP and UDP packets is preserved through a technique called Checksum Neutrality Preservation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each customer's router learns an IPv4 range from its IPv6 address. When sending IPv4 packets, it wraps them in IPv6 format, travels through the IPv6 network, and the gateway unwraps them back to IPv4.

sections.title: Address Assignment and Sharing
sections.content:
Customers can be assigned IPv4 addresses in three ways. First, a customer can receive a full public IPv4 address when the provider has enough IPv4 space. Second, a customer can receive one of several public IPv4 addresses. Third, in the case of IPv4 address scarcity, a customer can share a public IPv4 address with other customers, each receiving a restricted set of ports (the Address plus Port or A+P approach defined in RFC 6346).

When addresses are shared, the CE includes a Port-Set Identifier (PSID) in its mapping rule, which determines which ports belong to that customer. A local NAT44 (IPv4-to-IPv4 Network Address Translator) on the CE ensures that only packets using the assigned ports are sent to the carrier.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers get an IPv4 address or a part of one, like getting mailbox numbers 1-100 while another customer gets 101-200. A device at the customer site makes sure outgoing packets use only the allowed port numbers.

sections.title: Reversible Header Translation
sections.content:
4rd reversibly translates IPv4 headers into IPv6 headers using a technique that embeds IPv4 information into IPv6 fields. The IPv4 source and destination addresses are mapped to IPv6 addresses by replacing the Rule IPv4 prefix with a Rule IPv6 prefix. Other IPv4 fields like the Type of Service (TOS), Identification, and the Don't Fragment flag are placed in the IPv6 flow label and (when needed) the IPv6 fragment header.

At domain entry, an IPv4 packet with options is discarded because 4rd cannot translate options. At domain exit, the IPv6 packet is precisely reversed back to the original IPv4 packet, with one small exception: packets 68 octets or shorter always have their Don't Fragment flag set to 1, because such packets cannot be fragmented anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv4 address is turned into an IPv6 address, and extra IPv4 information is stored in unused IPv6 fields. When the packet exits, everything is reversed exactly, putting the IPv4 packet back together.

sections.title: Packet Flow and Topology
sections.content:
IPv4 packets are tunneled across the 4rd domain in either a mesh or hub-and-spoke topology. In mesh mode, CE-to-CE packets take direct IPv6 routes between the customer sites. In hub-and-spoke mode, all CE-to-CE traffic flows through one or more BRs. Both modes preserve IPv4 fragmentation rules end-to-end, ensuring that applications relying on Path MTU Discovery work correctly.

The IPv4 Time To Live (TTL) decreases normally during domain traversal, which is acceptable because the change is invisible to end-to-end TCP/UDP communication (the TTL does not affect the packet payload). The Domain Path MTU (minimum 1280 octets for IPv6) must be sufficient to carry the tunneled packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets can travel directly between customers or go through the provider's central relay. The packet size and fragment rules stay the same as if IPv4 went directly, so applications work normally.
